Fit: how Tom works, what he brings, what he is not for

The work he is best at

source: Tom's own account

I'm a fixer. I work on the really difficult stuff, the problems that are too hard or too messy for most people to get moving, and I like to solve them and move on. Once something is solved and running, I pass it to someone who's good at the routine work, and I go and find the next hard thing.

That pattern runs through my whole career: the domain search at Host Europe, the TREAT turnaround and closure, the Wegovycare discovery phase nobody wanted, the CagriSema funnel across two therapy areas that ran independently.

So if you have something stuck, broken, or blank-page, that's where I'm useful. If you need someone to run a mature product in steady state for years, it deserves someone who loves that, and it isn't me.

Organisation: where he works well

source: Tom's own account

I've worked in a 12-person startup (Opbeat, sharing an office with the founders), a scale-up through two acquisitions (Host Europe, Pipex), an innovation lab inside a pharma company (LEO), a 70,000-person corporate (Novo Nordisk) and on my own as a consultant. Size doesn't decide it.

What does: new things ship regularly, direct communication is welcome, you can rock the boat without fear of retribution, decisions get made on outcomes and evidence rather than on whose idea it was, and the organisation is leaning in to AI. Give me that and the freedom to act, and I'll do well.

To check this against your organisation, tell my agent how you work: stage, pace, how decisions get made, remote or not, what's broken. Five lines is enough.

Team: what he brings

source: Tom's own account

Ask the people I've worked with: kind, caring and fun; approachable; a structured mind; someone people come to when they want to spar on something messy. I bring energy and pace, I'm direct, and I work across silos without needing authority over them. I'm technical enough to lead ML teams and build with Claude Code, but my value is bridging disciplines, not writing production code, so I work with engineers best when they're close to the problem and the user, not handed tickets.

What I need around me: someone who loves the details and will bring up the overlooked fact, because I move fast and start more than I finish; a team that's prepared and to the point; and people who'll hold me to a completion date.

I've led teams of 5 to 15 and been the senior IC on others; both work. What I'd add depends on what your team already has, so tell my agent what the team does and what's missing, and ask again.

What he needs from leadership

source: Tom's own account

Freedom on the what and the how, clarity on the outcome and the date. Tell me where the prospects and opportunities lie and let me call a spade a spade.

Give me room to run discovery before building: if "you're not working if you're not coding" is the culture, we'll clash for a few months before it pays off, as it did at Novo. Trust early, because I'll use it to tell you things you may not want to hear, like recommending we close the flagship product. And tell me when my pace is wearing people out; I don't always notice.

What he is not a fit for

source: Tom's own account

Not a specialist engineer or a designer by trade any more: those are chapters, not the job. Marketing, growth and go-to-market are in scope when they sit inside a product or commercial role; a marketing-only seat is not the fit. Not a role that is mostly line management and levels; I can manage people and enjoy it, but it's not what gets me out of bed. Not a mature product in steady state; I'm a fixer, and once it's running it deserves someone who loves running it. And not a role that needs a decade in your exact domain: I move across industries on purpose and pick them up fast.
